chunks: Muhammad ibn Ali Majiluyah (may God be pleased with him) narrated to us, saying: My uncle Muhammad ibn Abi al-Qasim narrated to me, from Ahmad ibn Abi Abdullah al-Barqi, from his father Muhammad ibn Khalid, from Muhammad ibn Sinan, from Ibrahim ibn [Abi] Ziyad, from Abu Abdullah (peace be upon him), saying:

Indeed, God, the Blessed and Exalted, sent down an angel to the Earth, and he remained there for a long period. Then he was ascended to the heaven, and it was said to him: 'What did you see?' He said: 'I saw many wonders, and the most wonderful thing I saw was that I saw a servant moving about in Your blessings, eating Your sustenance, and claiming lordship. I was amazed at his boldness toward You, and at Your forbearance with him.' God, the Almighty, said: 'You were amazed at My forbearance?' He said: 'Yes [O Lord].' He said: 'I delayed him for four hundred years; no sweat of illness struck him, and he desired nothing from the world except that he attained it, and his food and drink did not change for him therein.'
ai.seo_question: What does the hadith say about the angel's observation of a servant claiming divinity while enjoying God's blessings?
ai.summary: In *Al-Khisal*, Shaykh al-Saduq uses this narrative to illustrate the concept of *tadallu* (divine stretching out of provision) as a test for the arrogant, where prolonged comfort serves as a precursor to reckoning. The angel’s wonder at God’s *hilm* (forbearance) specifically highlights the paradox of divine patience allowing a servant to consume God’s sustenance while falsely claiming lordship, a key theme in Shia exegesis regarding the nature of worldly power.
